CHAPTER 12: FISCAL POLICY AND THE BUDGET FRAMEWORK

INTRODUCTION
- This chapter covers the government budget, fiscal policy, the general government debt and privatisation. Study it with Chapter 7 (government aims and intervention).

GOVERNMENT CURRENT REVENUE
- According to the CSO, 73.6% of government current revenue in 2019 came from taxation. Taxation is the main source.
- Direct taxes: taxes on incomes and wealth. Examples: USC, PAYE, corporation tax, Capital Gains Tax (CGT), Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT), DIRT.
- Indirect taxes: taxes on goods/services (taxes on spending), paid indirectly to the government by final consumers. Examples: VAT, excise duty, carbon tax, Sugar-Sweetened Drinks Tax (SSDT).
- Some taxes are also used to correct market failure, e.g. sugar tax, carbon tax, tobacco taxes.

THE CANONS (PRINCIPLES) OF TAXATION - ADAM SMITH
- Developed by Scottish economist Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations (1776).
- 1. Equity: taxes should be fair - those who earn more pay more. PAYE is progressive, with a standard rate and a higher rate above the cut-off point.
- 2. Economy: tax should be cheap to collect; it should not cost more to collect than is raised (e.g. spending 100m to collect 90m breaks this rule).
- 3. Convenience: easy for the taxpayer to pay. E.g. local property tax can be paid by phone, online, by post, deducted from wages or welfare, at the bank or post office.
- 4. Certainty: taxpayers should know what they owe. Budget day is in October; most changes start on 1 January and then stay for at least 12 months. The government can also plan spending from predicted revenue.

THE MAIN TAXES
1. VAT (Value Added Tax)
- An indirect tax on goods/services paid by final consumers.
- Standard rate cut from 23% to 21% for six months from September 2020 to support businesses after the Covid-19 fall in demand.
- The 13.5% rate for tourism and hospitality (e.g. restaurant meals, hotels) cut to 9% during the pandemic so firms could lower prices.
- Top rate goods: motor vehicles, electrical goods, motor fuel, household goods, adult clothing, solicitors' fees.
- VAT is regressive. Regressive tax: does not take account of ability to pay; takes a higher percentage of a low earner's income than a high earner's.
- Example: 100 euro VAT is 33.3% of a 300 euro weekly income but only 16.6% of a 600 euro weekly income.

2. Excise duty
- Levied on tobacco, alcohol and fuel.
- Reasons: tobacco and alcohol seen as unnecessary; all three harmful (health or environment); higher prices reduce consumption.
- Regressive, like VAT.
- Figures: about 55c on a pint of lager; about 8.50 euro on 20 cigarettes; excise plus VAT is around 11 euro of a box of cigarettes.
- December 2020 fuel: diesel pump price 119.00c (excise + carbon tax 51.902c, VAT 20.65c, price before taxes 44.448c); petrol pump price 127.30c (excise + carbon tax 62.771c, VAT 22.09c, price before taxes 40.439c). NORA (National Oil Reserve Agency) 2c, set up to manage Ireland's strategic oil reserves.

3. USC (Universal Social Charge)
- Introduced in 2011.
- 2021: income under 12,000 euro exempt. Above that, bands: 0.5% up to 12,012; 2% from 12,012 to 20,687; 4.5% from 20,687 to 70,044; 8% over 70,044; 11% on self-employed income over 100,000. (No need to memorise rates.)
- A disincentive to work as it reduces take-home pay.
- Raises around 4 billion euro a year.
- Progressive. Progressive tax: takes account of ability to pay; takes a higher percentage from high earners than low earners.

4. PRSI (Pay Related Social Insurance)
- Goes into a social insurance fund that pays for social insurance benefits.
- Contributions depend on your PRSI 'class', which decides your entitlements, e.g. contributory state pension, jobseeker's benefit, illness benefit.
- Employers also pay employers' PRSI per employee, raising the cost of labour.

5. PAYE (Pay As You Earn)
- 2021 (single person): standard rate 20% up to the standard rate cut-off point of 35,300 euro; higher rate 40% above it.
- Progressive.
- Tax credit: money offset against your tax liability; depends on your circumstances.
- USC, PAYE and PRSI reduce disposable income.
- 2020 example: 30,000 euro earner - PAYE 2,700 after 3,300 credits, PRSI 1,200, USC 673, total 4,573, net 25,427. 60,000 euro earner - PAYE 13,640, PRSI 2,400, USC 2,023, total 18,063, net 41,937. Double the income pays about four times the tax, so direct taxes on labour are progressive.

6. SSDT (Sugar-Sweetened Drinks Tax)
- Came in 2018. 5-8g of sugar per 100ml: extra 20c per litre. Over 8g per 100ml: extra 30c per litre.

7. LPT (Local Property Tax)
- Introduced in 2013 to broaden the tax base (tax more areas) and replace revenue lost when the property market collapsed.
- Rates: 0.18% of market value up to 1 million euro; 0.25% on the part above 1 million. Based on the owner's 2013 valuation up to 2021, so bills did not rise with prices.
- Examples: 50,000 euro home - 90 euro a year; 225,000 euro - 405 euro; 975,000 euro - 1,755 euro.
- Implications: large, stable revenue (around 500 million euro a year) for local authorities (libraries, parks, street bins); not a disincentive to work - an alternative to higher USC/PAYE; equity argument - richer people live in dearer homes; inequity argument - a dear home does not mean high income; a high-income rural household could pay less than a low-income urban household; economy and convenience - cheap to collect and many ways to pay.

8. Carbon tax
- A charge on carbon-emitting fuels (coal, oil, natural gas). First introduced in 2010 to reduce emissions and support a greener environment.
- 2021: raised from 26 euro to 33.50 euro per tonne of CO2; to rise 7.50 euro a year to 100 euro per tonne by 2030. Raises fossil fuel prices.
- Examples: 5-6 euro of a 60-litre fill of fuel; about 80c of a bale of briquettes.

9. DIRT (Deposit Interest Retention Tax)
- A tax on interest. 41% in 2014, cut to 33% by 2020, 33% in 2021.
- Example: 100 euro at 10% interest earns 10 euro; 33% (3.33 euro) goes to the Revenue Commissioners.
- Reasons for a high rate: more revenue; convenience; economy (banks deduct and forward it, so collection is cheap); discourages saving and encourages spending, boosting national income.
- Inequitable and regressive: one rate whatever the saver's income.

10. Stamp duty
- A tax on certain transactions and instruments. Residential property 2021: 1% up to 1 million euro, 2% on the balance. A 200,000 euro home means 2,000 euro stamp duty, paid by the buyer.
- Instruments: credit cards 30 euro a year; combined ATM/debit cards 5 euro a year (2021).

11. CGT (Capital Gains Tax)
- Tax on the gain from selling an asset at a higher price than was paid, e.g. a second property. 33% in 2021, with exemptions.

12. CAT (Capital Acquisitions Tax)
- Tax on gifts and inheritance. 33% in 2021, only above a threshold.

13. Corporation tax
- A tax on company profits, paid by Irish companies and foreign-owned companies incorporated in Ireland.
- Rates: Ireland 12.5%; France 28-31%; UK 19% (rising to 25% in 2023); USA 21%.
- The low rate is a key reason Ireland attracts Foreign Direct Investment (FDI).
- Controversial: other EU countries miss out on FDI; many MNCs put European HQs here; US authorities criticised US firms for it.
- As of 2021 there were plans (resisted by Ireland) for a minimum global corporation tax of 15%.
- Apple: in Ireland since 1980, over 6,000 workers. The European Commission found Revenue tax rulings since 1991 lowered Apple's tax unfairly - illegal under EU state aid rules - and said Apple owed 13 billion euro plus interest. Not resolved when the book was published.

14. Plastic bag levy
- Introduced 2002 at 15c a bag; 22c in 2021. Retailers forward it to the Revenue Commissioners; money goes to environmental projects. Before 2002 bags were free.

15. Motor tax
- Mainly funds local authorities. A complementary good to buying a car. Expected to rise for petrol and diesel cars to encourage EVs; EV motor tax was 120 euro a year (2021).

OTHER TAX TERMS
- Tax avoidance: LEGALLY arranging your affairs to pay less tax, e.g. not saving in a bank to avoid DIRT.
- Tax evasion: ILLEGALLY reducing tax, e.g. not declaring income to the Revenue Commissioners.
- Impact of a tax: the initial burden - who the tax is first levied on.
- Incidence of a tax: who actually ends up paying it.
- Example: a 1% levy on insurance companies' revenue - the companies feel the impact, but if they raise premiums by 1% the incidence falls on customers (burden shifted).

GOVERNMENT CURRENT EXPENDITURE
- Figure 12.1 shows 2020 spending by area: social protection, health, education, justice, agriculture, debt servicing/EU payments, transport and other. Social protection is the biggest.
- 1. Public sector pay: 18.7 billion euro in 2019. Over 330,000 public sector workers (teachers, nurses, civil servants, local authority workers, Gardaí, defence forces).
  - Pay agreements link pay rises to productivity and the state of public finances; agreements with trade unions reduce industrial unrest (strikes).
  - After the 2008 crash, pay was cut and a pension levy imposed; the next decade was mostly about pay restoration.
- 2. Social welfare (transfer payments: payments for which no factor of production is provided).
  - Child benefit: 140 euro per month in 2021; universal (paid regardless of income).
  - Jobseeker's allowance: 203 euro a week aged 25+; 112.70 euro aged 18-24 not living independently (2021).
  - Disability allowance: 203 euro a week.
  - Department of Social Protection spent 21.3 billion euro in 2020 (around 26% of government spending). Pensions were the largest part (8.43 billion), followed by working age income supports and illness, disability and carers.

THE GOVERNMENT CURRENT BUDGET
- Budget day is in early October. Some changes start at midnight (e.g. fuel and cigarette taxes); most start on 1 January.
- Government current revenue: money collected on a continuous (day-to-day) basis, e.g. taxes (USC, VAT, corporation tax) and charges/fees (driving tests, prescription charges, speeding fines).
- Government current expenditure: money spent day-to-day, e.g. public sector pay, social welfare, servicing (paying interest on) the national debt, running costs of departments (stationery, light and heat, insurance, office rent).
- Budget 2019: revenue 87.5bn minus expenditure 86.1bn = +1.4bn, a current budget surplus.
- Current budget surplus (CBS): current revenue greater than current expenditure.
- Current budget deficit (CBD): current revenue less than current expenditure.
- Balanced budget: current revenue equals current expenditure.

IMPLICATIONS OF A CBD
- National debt rises; must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers.
- Economic growth is higher, as more is injected than withdrawn.
- Can cause overheating and inflation.
- The economy is more vulnerable to a shock with no surplus set aside.
- Risk of breaking EU rules (deficit max 3% of GDP, debt max 60% of GDP).

IMPLICATIONS OF A CBS
- Can reduce the general government debt and future interest costs.
- Economic growth is lower, as more is withdrawn than injected.
- Reduces inflation pressure and dampens demand if the economy risks overheating.
- Can be saved for a 'rainy day' - the government entered Covid-19 with a CBS of 1.4bn.
- Pressure to spend the surplus, e.g. pay claims, welfare increase demands.

HOW THE GOVERNMENT REDUCED THE CBD (AUSTERITY)
- After the 2008 crash, tax revenue fell sharply (unemployment, property collapse) and welfare spending rose. Deficits ran until 2018.
- Austerity: continuously raising current revenue and cutting current spending.
- Raising revenue: USC (2011); LPT (2013); standard VAT up from 21% to 23%; carbon tax (2010) with annual rises; higher DIRT; new charges such as prescription charges for medical card holders.
- Cutting spending: public sector recruitment ban; lower pay bill (e.g. less overtime for Gardaí and health workers); cuts to child benefit and jobseeker's allowance (halved for under-25s); third-level registration fee raised to 3,000 euro; cuts to services (closing some A&E departments and Garda stations).
- Effects of austerity: growth in the hidden economy (cash work, smuggled cigarettes); poorer state services (fewer health workers, longer waiting lists); more emigration (push factors); lower demand due to lower disposable income (USC, pension levy); more inequality (higher labour taxes on low earners, charges hitting the vulnerable, 3,000 euro fee a barrier to college).
- CBD eliminated in 2018 (surplus of 400m). CBS 2019 = 1.4bn. Covid-19 caused a CBD of around 20bn in 2020.

FISCAL POLICY
- Policy: a plan or course of action used to achieve an aim.
- Fiscal policy: government actions that influence the timing, magnitude and structure of government current revenue and current expenditure.
- Expansionary fiscal policy: used in a downturn (e.g. to reach full employment). Raise government spending and cut taxes on labour to raise disposable income, aggregate demand and employment. Usually needs a CBD funded by borrowing.
- Limits on borrowing: the NTMA must be able to borrow at low interest rates; EU Stability and Growth Pact (SGP) - deficits under 3% of GDP, debt under 60% of GDP (relaxed during Covid-19). Budget plans need EU pre-approval. EU state aid rules stop a government giving a big grant to save one firm, as this is unfair to competitors (anti-competitive).
- Contractionary fiscal policy: used when growth is rapid with inflation and capacity constraints. Cut government spending (aim for a CBS) and raise taxes on labour to cut disposable income and aggregate demand.
- Capacity constraints: factors stopping a business producing more, e.g. shortages of raw materials or labour.
- Fiscal neutrality: current revenue equals current spending; demand is neither stimulated nor reduced.

USING FISCAL POLICY TO STABILISE THE BUSINESS CYCLE
- Diagram (Figure 12.3) in words: real GDP on the vertical axis, time on the horizontal; a wave rises to peaks and falls to troughs around a rising trend line.
- In expansion/peak: use contractionary policy to prevent overheating, high inflation, asset bubbles and capacity constraints. In the late Celtic Tiger years the government did the wrong thing - it raised spending and kept taxes low, adding to the property bubble and inflation.
- In contraction/trough: use expansionary policy. Budget 2021 borrowed around 25bn as a 'counter-cyclical measure' for Covid-19, e.g. the Pandemic Unemployment Payment of 350 euro a week and business supports.

LIMITATIONS OF FISCAL POLICY
- 1. Must be able to borrow large sums at affordable rates; a poor credit rating or high existing debt limits this.
- 2. A severe shock may be too big for fiscal policy to prevent a downturn.
- 3. EU rules (3% deficit, 60% debt) limit action (relaxed for Covid-19).
- 4. As a eurozone member, fiscal policy should be consistent with ECB monetary policy; e.g. if the ECB raised rates to fight inflation, a contractionary fiscal policy might be needed.
- 5. Expectations/confidence: pessimistic workers may save a tax cut rather than spend it.
- 6. Open economy: much of an injection may be spent on imports, so national income rises less.

THE GOVERNMENT CAPITAL BUDGET
- Project Ireland 2040: a 116 billion euro capital investment plan for housing, transport, roads, ports, airports, broadband, schools and hospitals. Depends on the economy, private investment and EU funding.
- Capital expenditure: usually once-off spending on assets used for generations; raises living standards, future productive capacity and attractiveness for FDI. Examples: National Children's Hospital, Cork-Limerick Motorway, Metro North, Galway bypass.
- Capital income: once-off income, e.g. privatisation (335m for the Aer Lingus share in 2015; 405m for the National Lottery licence), EU grants for infrastructure.
- The capital budget is announced with the current budget on budget day.

THE NATIONAL DEBT
- National debt: the total government debt outstanding. Also called general government debt (GGD), used by the CSO and NTMA and for EU comparisons.
- Includes: debt built up from past CBDs; debt of central and local government bodies; money borrowed to support banks in the financial crisis.
- GGD was 226.4bn in January 2021 (NTMA); borrowing rose sharply in 2020-2021.
- Table 12.10: 2016 - 201bn, 74%, interest 6.264bn; 2017 - 201bn, 67%, 5.941bn; 2018 - 206bn, 63%, 5.318bn; 2019 - 204bn, 57%, 4.457bn.
- Debt/GDP ratio: size of debt relative to the economy; the lower the better. Fell from a high of 120% (2012-2013) to 57% in 2019; rose again with Covid-19.
- Interest comes from current tax revenue. 2019 interest of almost 4.5bn = about nine years of property tax, or more than a year's USC.

HOW THE GOVERNMENT BORROWS - THE NTMA AND BONDS
- The National Treasury Management Agency (NTMA) borrows for the state and manages the GGD.
- It holds an auction: it says it wants to borrow (e.g. 6bn over 10 years); investment funds, cash-rich firms and wealthy individuals offer to lend. More offers mean a lower interest rate (bond yield), reducing the taxpayer's burden.
- The yield is paid yearly from current revenue; the capital is repaid at the end.
- Selling a bond = borrowing. Buying a bond = lending. A bond is a loan receipt (like an IOU); the lender is a bondholder. Prize bond owners are bondholders lending to the government.
- June 2020 press release: NTMA raised 6bn with a 10-year bond maturing October 2030 at a yield of 0.285%. Orders of around 66bn from over 400 accounts - Ireland seen as a safe place to invest even in Covid-19.
- In 2010, during the financial crisis, Ireland was high-risk; yields were over 9%, unaffordable. The government turned to the troika, whose loans required austerity.

IMPLICATIONS OF A LARGE NATIONAL DEBT
- Borrowing lets the government inject more than it withdraws in a downturn.
- 1. Cost: repaid with interest by future taxpayers; close to 22bn paid in interest 2016-2019.
- 2. Opportunity cost (the best alternative foregone): interest could fund health, education, welfare, or maybe abolish USC. The 4.5bn in 2019 would have paid for two hospitals like the National Children's Hospital.
- 3. Borrowing for current spending is unsustainable (like a loan for weekly shopping); borrowing should ideally be for once-off capital purposes.
- 4. High debt makes the country vulnerable to shocks and limits its ability to borrow in a recession.
- 5. Borrowing can be counter-cyclical, making a contraction less severe.

FUNCTIONS OF THE NTMA
- Main job: manage the national debt, including 'rolling over the debt' (replacing old high-interest loans with new lower-interest ones).
- 1. State Claims Agency: manages claims against the state.
- 2. Dormant Accounts Fund: manages money left in dormant accounts.
- 3. NewEra: financial and commercial advice on state and semi-state companies.
- 4. NAMA (National Asset Management Agency): NTMA gives it staff and support; NAMA bought and managed property loans from banks in the crisis.
- 5. ISIF (Ireland Strategic Investment Fund): about 8bn invested for a return while supporting Irish jobs, e.g. Abbey Quarter in Kilkenny, West Cork Distillers.

PRIVATISATION
- Privatisation: the sale of a state-owned firm to private investors.
- Already privatised: Irish Sugar, Irish Ferries, Telecom Eireann (now Eir), the National Lottery (Premier Lotteries Ireland, 20-year licence), Aer Lingus (remaining share sold to International Airlines Group, IAG, in 2015).
- Could be privatised: Electric Ireland (formerly ESB), Bord Gais, Coillte, Bord na Mona, Dublin Bus, Irish Rail, Bus Eireann.
Arguments for:
- 1. Once-off capital payment: the National Lottery licence raised 405m in 2014; some went to the National Children's Hospital.
- 2. Private firms are (in theory) more efficient: profit motive cuts costs/waste and ends loss-making activities.
- 3. Future losses are not a burden on the state, e.g. Aer Lingus's Covid-19 losses.
Arguments against:
- 1. Job losses as owners cut costs; unions resist loss of job security.
- 2. Future profits go to private owners (e.g. IAG) not the exchequer.
- 3. Higher prices, e.g. National Lottery game prices rose soon after the takeover.
- 4. Cuts to services that matter to customers but are not profitable.
- 5. State loses control of strategic firms, e.g. without Telecom Eireann it could not roll out national high-speed broadband; many areas have poor broadband.

rows.prompt: Which of these is a DIRECT tax?
rows.explanation: Direct taxes are on incomes and wealth, e.g. PAYE, USC, corporation tax.

rows.prompt: In 2019, what share of government current revenue came from taxation (CSO)?
rows.explanation: The CSO states 73.6% of current revenue in 2019 came from taxation.

rows.prompt: Who developed the four canons of taxation?
rows.explanation: Adam Smith set them out in The Wealth of Nations (1776).

rows.prompt: Local property tax can be paid online, by phone or through wage deductions. Which canon does this show?
rows.explanation: Convenience means a tax should be easy for the taxpayer to pay.

rows.prompt: It costs €100m to collect €90m in a tax. Which canon is broken?
rows.explanation: Economy means a tax should be cheap to collect, never costing more than it raises.

rows.prompt: Why is VAT described as a regressive tax?
options: It takes a higher percentage of a low earner's income than a high earner's
It takes a higher percentage of a high earner's income than a low earner's
It is charged only on goods bought by companies
It falls in value when inflation rises
rows.explanation: VAT ignores ability to pay: €100 VAT is 33.3% of €300 but only 16.6% of €600.

rows.prompt: Excise duties are levied on which group of products?
rows.explanation: The chapter states excise duties are levied on tobacco, alcohol and fuel.

rows.prompt: In which year was the Universal Social Charge introduced?
rows.explanation: The USC was introduced in 2011.

rows.prompt: What is the 2021 standard rate cut-off point for PAYE for a single person?
rows.explanation: Income up to €35,300 is taxed at 20%; above it at 40%.

rows.prompt: A worker on €60,000 paid about four times the tax of a worker on €30,000. What does this show?
options: Direct taxes on labour are regressive
Direct taxes on labour are progressive
rows.explanation: Paying a higher share as income rises means the tax is progressive.

rows.prompt: A drink has over 8g of sugar per 100ml. How much extra does the SSDT add?
rows.explanation: Drinks with over 8g per 100ml pay 30c per litre; 5-8g pay 20c per litre.

rows.prompt: What was the original LPT rate on market value up to €1 million?
rows.explanation: LPT was 0.18% up to €1m and 0.25% on the portion above.

rows.prompt: Which is an argument AGAINST the fairness of the local property tax?
options: It provides a stable source of revenue for local councils
It is cheap for local authorities to collect
It does not act as a disincentive to work
Living in a dear house does not mean you have the income to pay
rows.explanation: Critics argue an expensive property does not necessarily mean a high income.

rows.prompt: The carbon tax is expected to reach what level by 2030?
rows.explanation: It is expected to rise by €7.50 a year until it reaches €100 per tonne by 2030.

rows.prompt: You earn €10 interest and DIRT is 33%. How much DIRT is deducted?
rows.explanation: 33% of €10 is €3.33, deducted by the bank and sent to Revenue.

rows.prompt: Capital Acquisitions Tax (CAT) is a tax on:
rows.explanation: CAT applies to gifts and inheritance above a threshold.

rows.prompt: What is Ireland's rate of corporation tax given in the chapter?
rows.explanation: Ireland's rate is 12.5%, compared with 21% in the USA and 19% in the UK.

rows.prompt: Why did the European Commission say Apple owed €13 billion plus interest?
options: Apple had evaded VAT on its Irish sales
Revenue tax rulings were illegal state aid under EU rules
Apple had not paid PRSI for its Irish staff
Apple had broken the EU plastic bag levy rules
rows.explanation: The Commission found rulings since 1991 lowered Apple's tax unfairly, which is illegal under EU state aid rules.

rows.prompt: Not declaring income to the Revenue Commissioners is an example of:
rows.explanation: Tax evasion is the illegal reduction of tax, e.g. not declaring income.

rows.prompt: A levy is placed on insurers, who then raise premiums by the same amount. Who bears the incidence?
rows.explanation: Impact is the initial burden (insurers); incidence is who finally pays (customers).

rows.prompt: Current revenue is €87.5bn and current expenditure is €86.1bn. What is the result?
rows.explanation: Revenue greater than expenditure gives a surplus: 87.5 - 86.1 = €1.4bn (Budget 2019).

rows.prompt: Which of these is government CURRENT expenditure?
rows.explanation: Current spending is day-to-day, e.g. pay, welfare and debt interest; the others are capital spending.

rows.prompt: Which is an implication of a current budget deficit?
rows.explanation: A deficit means spending more than is taken in, so borrowing and the national debt rise.

rows.prompt: Which measure was used to INCREASE government current revenue during austerity?
rows.explanation: LPT (2013) raised revenue; the others were ways of cutting spending.

rows.prompt: What is fiscal policy?
options: Central bank actions on interest rates and the money supply
EU rules on trade between member states
Bank decisions on how much credit to give firms
Government actions on the timing, size and structure of current revenue and spending
rows.explanation: Fiscal policy concerns government current revenue and current expenditure.

rows.prompt: Which is part of an EXPANSIONARY fiscal policy?
rows.explanation: Expansionary policy raises spending and cuts taxes to boost aggregate demand.

rows.prompt: Why might a cut in taxes during a recession have little effect?
options: Pessimistic workers may save the extra income
Workers must pay the money back to the government
Lower taxes always cause higher inflation
The ECB forbids tax cuts during a recession
rows.explanation: Low confidence limits fiscal policy: people may save rather than spend extra disposable income.

rows.prompt: When the NTMA 'sells a bond', it is:
rows.explanation: Selling a bond means borrowing; buying a bond means lending.

rows.prompt: In June 2020 the NTMA raised €6bn at a yield of 0.285%. Why was the yield so low?
options: The ECB set the bond yield for all eurozone states
Investors offered about €66bn, competing to lend
Ireland had a large current budget surplus that year
The troika lent the money at a fixed low rate
rows.explanation: Strong demand from over 400 accounts meant lenders competed, pushing the yield down.

rows.prompt: Which is an argument FOR privatisation?
options: Future profits go to private owners
The state loses control of a strategic firm
The state receives a once-off capital payment
rows.explanation: E.g. the National Lottery licence raised €405m; the others are arguments against.

rows.prompt: State and explain the four canons of taxation.
rows.model_answer: Equity - taxes should be fair, so those who earn more pay more (e.g. PAYE's two rates). Economy - a tax should be cheap to collect. Convenience - easy to pay, e.g. LPT by phone or wage deduction. Certainty - taxpayers know what they owe, as budget changes usually last at least 12 months.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between a progressive and a regressive tax, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: A progressive tax takes account of ability to pay, taking a higher percentage from high earners, e.g. PAYE or USC. A regressive tax ignores ability to pay and takes a higher percentage of a low earner's income, e.g. VAT - €100 VAT is 33.3% of a €300 income but 16.6% of a €600 income.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between tax avoidance and tax evasion, and between the impact and incidence of a tax.
rows.model_answer: Tax avoidance is legally arranging your affairs to pay less tax; tax evasion is doing so illegally, e.g. not declaring income. Impact is the initial burden, on whoever the tax is levied; incidence is who actually ends up paying, e.g. insurers passing a levy on to customers.

rows.prompt: Define a current budget deficit, a current budget surplus and a balanced budget.
rows.model_answer: A current budget deficit is when government current revenue is less than current expenditure. A surplus is when current revenue is greater than current expenditure. A balanced budget is when they are equal.

rows.prompt: Give two ways the government raised revenue and two ways it cut spending to eliminate the deficit after 2008.
rows.model_answer: To raise revenue it introduced the USC (2011) and the local property tax (2013); it also raised VAT to 23% and brought in the carbon tax. To cut spending it imposed a public sector recruitment ban and cut social welfare payments such as jobseeker's allowance for under-25s.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy.
rows.model_answer: Expansionary fiscal policy increases government spending and cuts taxes on labour to boost aggregate demand and employment in a downturn, usually with a deficit. Contractionary fiscal policy cuts spending and raises taxes to reduce demand when the economy is overheating, aiming for a surplus.

rows.prompt: Explain how the NTMA borrows money by selling a bond.
rows.model_answer: The NTMA announces it wants to borrow, e.g. €6bn over 10 years. Investors offer to lend; the more offers, the lower the yield (interest). Interest is paid yearly out of current revenue and the capital is repaid at the end. The lender holds the bond and is a bondholder.

rows.prompt: Define privatisation and give two arguments against it.
rows.model_answer: Privatisation is the sale of a state-owned firm to private investors. Against: job losses as profit-driven owners cut costs, and future profits go to private owners (e.g. IAG for Aer Lingus) instead of the exchequer. Prices may also rise, as with National Lottery games.

rows.prompt: Explain how the government can use fiscal policy to stabilise the business cycle, and discuss the limitations of fiscal policy for Ireland. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: In the expansion or peak phase the government should use contractionary fiscal policy - cutting spending, aiming for a surplus and raising taxes on labour - to prevent overheating, high inflation and asset bubbles. In the late Celtic Tiger years it did the opposite, raising spending and keeping taxes low, which fed the property bubble. In the contraction or trough it should use expansionary policy - more spending and lower taxes - to boost demand. In Budget 2021 it borrowed around €25bn as a counter-cyclical measure, funding the €350 Pandemic Unemployment Payment. Limitations: it must be able to borrow at affordable rates, which is hard with a poor credit rating or high debt. EU rules limit deficits to 3% and debt to 60% of GDP. As a eurozone member, fiscal policy must be consistent with ECB monetary policy. Pessimistic consumers may save tax cuts instead of spending them. In an open economy like Ireland much of an injection leaks out as imports. A severe shock may be too big for fiscal policy alone.
rows.marking_scheme: Use in business cycle: 2 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation/example) = 10m. Limitations: 3 points x 5m (2m + 3m) = 15m.

rows.prompt: Discuss the economic implications for Ireland of running (i) a current budget deficit and (ii) a current budget surplus. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Deficit: the national debt rises and must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers. Growth is higher, as more is injected into the economy than withdrawn. It can cause overheating and inflation. The economy is more vulnerable to a shock with no surplus set aside, and it risks breaking EU rules if the deficit exceeds 3% of GDP. (ii) Surplus: it can be used to reduce the general government debt and future interest costs. Growth is lower as more is withdrawn than injected. It reduces inflation pressure if the economy risks overheating. It can be kept for a rainy day - Ireland entered Covid-19 with a surplus of €1.4bn. However, the government may face pressure for pay rises and higher welfare.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 2 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation). (ii) 2 points x 5m (2m + 3m).

rows.prompt: (a) Explain the term 'debt/GDP ratio'. (b) Discuss the economic implications for Ireland of a large national debt. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) The debt/GDP ratio shows the size of a country's debt relative to the size of its economy; the lower the better. Ireland's fell from 120% in 2012-2013 to 57% in 2019 before Covid-19 raised it. (b) The debt must be repaid with interest by future taxpayers - close to €22bn in interest was paid in 2016-2019. There is a large opportunity cost: the €4.5bn of interest in 2019 could have paid for two hospitals like the National Children's Hospital. Borrowing for day-to-day spending is unsustainable; borrowing should be for once-off capital projects. High debt leaves Ireland vulnerable to shocks and limits its ability to borrow in a recession, as in 2010 when yields topped 9% and Ireland turned to the troika. On the positive side, borrowing can be counter-cyclical.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 5m (2m definition + 3m explanation). (b) 3 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation).

rows.prompt: Discuss the arguments for and against the privatisation of a state-owned company. Refer to Irish examples. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: For: the state gets a once-off capital payment, e.g. €405m for the National Lottery licence in 2014, partly used for the National Children's Hospital. Private firms are, in theory, more efficient because the profit motive cuts waste and ends loss-making activities. Future losses are not a burden on the taxpayer, e.g. Aer Lingus's Covid-19 losses. Against: job losses as owners cut costs. Future profits go to private owners such as IAG rather than the exchequer. Prices may rise, as National Lottery game prices did. Services that are not profitable may be cut. The state loses control of strategic firms - without Telecom Eireann it could not roll out national broadband.
rows.marking_scheme: For: 2 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation with example). Against: 2 points x 5m (2m + 3m).
